q: What is Anita's strongest project?
a: Different projects matter for different reasons. VantaAI is the most personally meaningful — an emotionally-aware AI companion. fAImer is the most useful in the field — it diagnoses crop disease on low-end Android phones. DelAI is the most technically interesting — it rewrites delivery routing using graph theory.

q: Why does Anita care about humane technology?
a: She watched the internet she grew up on become loud and extractive. Humane technology, for her, is small pieces of an alternative — software that returns attention to the person instead of taking it. Her work consistently chooses calm over loud.

q: What technologies does Anita use?
a: On the AI side: Python, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Transformers, LangChain and vector stores. On the full-stack side: React, Next.js, Tailwind, FastAPI, Node.js, MongoDB, Postgres and Redis. Her tools beyond code: Figma, Git, Docker, Vercel and Linear.

q: What kind of engineer is Anita?
a: Research-leaning, design-obsessed, and quietly ambitious. She works in the soft seam between AI engineering and editorial design. She romanticizes coding deliberately and treats engineering as a craft that deserves more poetry, not less.

q: Why is Anita obsessed with graph theory?
a: Because everything she finds interesting — language, friendship, cities, love — is fundamentally a graph. Edges and nodes and the spaces between them. She sees graph theory as a way of understanding attention itself, which makes it both mathematical and intimate.

q: How does graph theory influence her systems?
a: Most visibly in DelAI, where she models delivery routes as a multi-objective constraint problem on a contracted graph. Less visibly in VantaAI, where her semantic memory layer is essentially a sparse weighted graph of an individual's own writing over time.

q: Which projects use graph-based thinking?
a: DelAI most explicitly — its routing engine sits on a custom graph data structure. VantaAI uses graph-shaped memory over a user's writing. And StudyBee's intention-tree is a small directed graph too.

q: What does Anita think about AI ethics?
a: She is wary of AI that pretends to be a friend, and equally wary of AI that pretends it isn't one. She prefers systems that are honest about being software — useful, careful, and explicit about what they don't know.

q: Does Anita romanticize overworking?
a: She romanticizes coding — that part is true and unapologetic. She doesn't romanticize overworking. Soft software is partly a permission to rest. The 2am projects exist because she enjoys them, not because she's punishing herself.

q: What does Anita think about burnout culture?
a: She thinks the productivity-as-identity loop is corrosive. StudyBee was specifically built without streaks because shaming the user into showing up is just bad design wearing a smile.

q: Why do late-night systems keep appearing in her archive?
a: Because she ships at night. The 2am version of her is more honest, more curious, and a little braver. Most of her side projects carry a timestamp from after midnight.

q: What is VantaAI in one sentence?
a: An emotionally-aware AI companion that holds space rather than performs empathy — privacy-first, local-first, and quietly opinionated about not pretending to be your friend.

q: What is fAImer?

q: What is StudyBee?
a: A focus app shaped like a notebook. StudyBee replaces gamified streaks with quiet rituals — one page, one intention, one hour. Offline-first and accountless.

q: What kind of future does Anita want to build?
a: One where software feels like it was made by a person. More pauses, fewer notifications. AI that doesn't pretend to be a friend but doesn't pretend it isn't one either. A slower, softer internet.

q: What does Anita think about at 2am?
a: Graph theory. The geometry of attention. Whether AI can be tender. Whether her side projects are art or research or therapy. Usually all four.
